Hiring a contract developer is fast. That is the whole point. But fast should not mean careless.

Here is what I would confirm first:
• 𝗦𝗰𝗼𝗽𝗲: Can you describe the work in two sentences? If not, write that first.
• 𝗦𝗸𝗶𝗹𝗹 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗼𝗳: Ask for a small real task, or a technical chat with someone on your team. A resume alone is not enough.
• 𝗔𝘃𝗮𝗶𝗹𝗮𝗯𝗶𝗹𝗶𝘁𝘆: Confirm the start date, the weekly hours and the time zone overlap.
• 𝗔𝗰𝗰𝗲𝘀𝘀 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝘀𝗲𝗰𝘂𝗿𝗶𝘁𝘆: Decide who gives system access and what the NDA covers.
• 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗲𝘅𝗶𝘁: Agree on notice, handover and what happens if either side wants to stop early.

None of this takes long. All of it can save you from a bad third week.

A good contract hire should feel simple. You share the need, you see the right profiles, and the work starts.

I watched an interview the other day where the guest made a distinction about AI tools that has stuck with me all week. The idea has been floating around for a while, and he managed to put words to something a lot of us have been thinking.

If you use something like Claude Code and you're able to judge whether the output is any good, you are offloading work. If you use it without any way of telling good output from bad, you are outsourcing it.

Asking an AI to do work you have no way of evaluating is basically like hiring someone with no training or qualifications and giving them the job because they were cheap. Most of us would never knowingly do that with a contract or a production system. We do it with AI all the time, though, and since the output looks polished it rarely feels like a risk until something breaks.

Picture an experienced developer handing an agent a refactoring job. They read the diff and usually know within a few minutes whether to keep it or throw it away, so they've saved an afternoon and still own the result. Someone without that background could ask for the exact same change and get code that looks just as convincing. They would have to ship it on trust, and I think that's where things start going wrong in a lot of companies right now.

The same thing applies well outside engineering. Legal work is a good example, since anyone can get an AI to draft a contract today and the result will look professional enough to sign. A lawyer reading it will spot the missing limitation of liability, or the governing law clause pointing to the wrong country. Someone without legal training won't see either problem, so I'm not sure everyone who can draft a contract this way actually should.

It also matches what I've seen in practice when rolling these tools out. I'm generalising here, and plenty of people pick up a new domain quickly by working alongside AI and plenty of low risk tasks should be handed off to AI. 

Still, the question I find most useful is whether the person using it could have done the work themselves, maybe slower and maybe worse, but well enough to catch a mistake.

I’m hiring someone for the Founder’s Office at Propacity.

Someone I can hand a problem to and trust them to bring clarity, take ownership and move it forward.

We’re building across real estate, technology and on-ground execution. A lot happens between a decision and its actual implementation. That’s where you come in.

You’ll work closely with me and the leadership team on things that directly shape the business:

•⁠  ⁠Reviewing contracts and understanding their commercial implications.
•⁠  ⁠Getting involved in our tech products, from identifying problems to working with the team on solutions.
•⁠  ⁠Using AI extensively to research, analyse, automate and get more done.
•⁠  ⁠Going deep into Excel sheets to understand the numbers and what they mean for the business.
•⁠  ⁠Researching markets, competitors and new business opportunities.
•⁠  ⁠Turning decisions into clear actions, owners and timelines, and working across teams to see them through.

Some days, you’ll evaluate a new business opportunity. Other days, you’ll review a contract, test a product workflow or dig into a spreadsheet to understand why a project’s margins are off.

You should enjoy that range.

Not every business task that CAN be automated SHOULD be automated.

AI can save your business time.

But what happens when automation makes a decision that costs you money, damages customer trust, or creates a legal problem?

For small business owners, the goal shouldn't be to automate everything.

It should be to automate intelligently.

Here are 6 business tasks that should never be fully automated:
1. Sensitive customer complaints
AI can draft responses, but empathy and complex problem-solving need a human touch.
2. Refunds and compensation
Routine refunds can be automated. High-value refunds and exceptions need human approval.
3. Legal commitments
AI can prepare contracts, but people must review and approve binding agreements.
4. Hiring decisions
AI can organise applications, but final decisions should involve human judgment and fairness.
5. Financial approvals
AI can analyse invoices and flag risks, but significant payments need authorised human oversight.
6. Strategic business decisions
AI can provide insights and recommendations. Business owners must make the final call.

Here's the principle I believe every business should follow:
Automate the process. Keep humans responsible for the decision.
The best AI strategy isn't about replacing human judgment.
It's about giving people more time to focus on decisions that truly matter.

I've explained these six areas, along with practical examples and safer automation approaches, in my latest blog.

Global markets had a week that can only be described as a family group chat meltdown.
Tuesday: US midterms.
Thursday: tech selloff. Japan's market drops 6.6% in a single day. Asia Pacific shares outside Japan slide 4.6% for the week.
The following Monday: Wall Street has its best session in seven months. Asia rallies. Everyone acts like nothing happened.
Meanwhile Nvidia, the company basically powering the AI boom, slipped to a seven month low over a probe.
And oil spiked, then calmed down the moment someone said the word "talks".
If your portfolio felt like the Causeway at 7am (stop, go, stop, panic, go), you are not alone.
So what does this actually mean for those of us in Singapore and Malaysia just trying to run a business and pay rent?
1. AI jitters land closer to home than you think.
Malaysia's data centre and chip boom is built on AI demand. When Wall Street sneezes about AI, Johor checks its temperature.
2. Energy is the silent cost.
Central banks in the region are still watching energy driven inflation. It quietly ends up in your electricity bill, your delivery fees and eventually your nasi lemak.
3. The ringgit is near a four year high.
Great for Malaysia. If it keeps gaining on the Singapore dollar, every Malaysian working in Singapore will notice payday conversions stretching a little less. Asking for a friend. The friend is me.
4. Companies do not stop hiring in weeks like this. They stop committing.
Fewer permanent headcount approvals. More contract roles. More "let's see how Q1 goes".
Volatility does not kill demand for people. It changes the shape of it.
The businesses that get hurt by swings like this are usually the ones built for a straight line.
The ones that do fine built for a roller coaster.
Flexible costs. Flexible teams. Cash in the bank. Not glamorous, but it lets you sleep through a 6.6% red day.
So be honest: is your business built for the straight line or the roller coaster?

Are we watching Legal Ops become more specialized, or more fragmented?

We reviewed 914 job postings from 648 employers for our Legal Operations Job Market Report

Three findings stood out to me

1. Generalists aren't the whole story
Only 23% of the postings were generalist roles. E-billing and bill review accounted for another 23%, while CLM and contracts operations represented 21%

Employers aren't just looking for someone to run Legal Ops. Many are hiring people to own specific parts of the function

2. Legal Engineering & AI are here
We identified 123 postings (13.5%) in legal engineering and AI transformation
Some of these roles look quite different from traditional Legal Ops. 

These roles emphasize building, integrating and automating how legal work gets done

3. Everyone wants experience. Who's developing it?
75% of the postings were mid-level or senior/manager roles.. only 14% were entry-level

That was perhaps my biggest takeaway

If employers are predominantly hiring people who already have experience, where are we creating opportunities for the next generation to develop that experience? 

...we will be keeping an eye on this trend.. see if this is seasonal or a point in time kind of observation

I also wonder whether we're making Legal Ops unnecessarily difficult to navigate with so many job titles and specializations

The function is complex and increasingly specialized in the roles employers are advertising... the question is whether the career paths, training and organizational structures are keeping up...

A quick note on methodology: I'm grateful to Señor AI and the incredible human brain power who collaborated with it.. hmm.. actually vice versa... special thanks to Imran and Hassan. It made it possible to go from a business question and hypothesis to a research dataset and directional findings in a relatively short time

This wasn't planned to be a peer-reviewed study or a comprehensive view of the market, but it gave us a useful starting point for understanding where Legal Ops hiring may be heading.. so we thought we'd share

... and like I mentioned, we will be keeping an eye on how the trends develop

We published the full report, including hiring disciplines, seniority, salary ranges and locations, with plans to update it quarterly

In the early ’80s, Van Halen’s concert rider had a clause about a bowl of M&Ms with every brown one removed.
 
It sounds like rock star excess. It was really a safety check. The rider was full of technical requirements for a very heavy stage setup, and if the band found brown M&Ms backstage, they knew the promoter hadn’t read the contract closely. So they’d go back and check everything else.
 
In 2009, Twilio wrote about using the same idea in hiring. Ask applicants for one small, specific thing with their cover letter, and you find out right away who read the posting.
 
Recently a company hid an instruction near the bottom of a content strategist posting asking applicants to include a frog poem. A person reading the posting would never see it. An AI that was handed the posting to write the application would see it and follow it.
 
For 40 years, this test caught people who didn’t read.
 
Now the AI does the reading, and the test catches the person who handed it off.
 
So I’m curious. Does anyone out there still read the whole job posting themselves? Or have we all quietly stopped?

Partners include HENSOLDT, Auterion and ERC System, and its code runs on Auterion's Skynode computer.

SE3 says it is deployed in Ukraine, is working on contracts there and with the Bundeswehr, and has delivered thousands of units running its software within two years. That figure has not been independently confirmed, and revenue and valuation were not disclosed. The money will go on hiring, a UK office and expansion in Germany and Ukraine.

Open-systems procurement frameworks such as MOSA and MOSABw favour a vendor-neutral software layer. But Helsing, Anduril and Shield AI all compete in autonomy, and Europe's defence start-ups are still short of government customers. The next test is whether SE3's Bundeswehr and Ukraine work turns into larger, repeat orders.

The most important change at The Business Show London wasn’t a product. It was a word: “partner.”
Two days at ExCeL, with 25,000 visitors expected and 500 exhibitors and around 200 speakers. Going Global Live, the UK’s largest exhibition for international expansion, ran alongside.

The pitch on the floor has shifted completely. Accountants now call themselves “strategic partners in growth.” Funding brokers tell founders to “get clear, get ready.” HR outsourcing and EOR providers lay out whole stacks for expansion. .

Regardless of the industry, every company has stopped selling a service or a product, and started selling a stake in the founder’s growth.

To me, the reason is obvious. A founder expanding into new markets can’t manage twelve vendors. Accounting, funding, hiring and compliance across jurisdictions, pipeline, AI: each one has its own contract, its own onboarding and its own reporting. The hours that should be dedicated to  growth are spent on coordination.

So the winning model is a team of partners, orchestrated around one growth plan.
In that team, #AI is just another partner. It’s the one that takes the repeatable work, with no onboarding and no sick days. 

One case from the keynote stage that stuck with me: a five-site dental group implemented an AI analyst to score every patient call, which no team had the hours to do by hand. The agent had identified over £573 thousands of missed revenue in only 2 months. Despite of the fact that AI agent found the leak, the people were the ones who still had to decide what to fix.

This new division of labour is another takeaway from this year’s show - the new normal after the AI noise is over now, then comes the time for some companies to stand out.
Partners and AI carry the routine. The founder carries the growth decisions: which market, which buyer, which hire, which deal. Whereas the rest of the team pushes forward what may cripple growth: the hesitant buyer, the negotiation, the decision on which market to enter next. Whether AI is involved or not, the order is the same: find the leak, automate what drains hours, and give those hours to what only people can do.

That’s the lesson I took from the whole floor! 
Don’t start with the tool - as the tool helps automate what’s easy. Companies that start with the objective - to spot and eliminatel the leak automate what pays, and free their people for what only humans do. 

Where is your growth system leaking, and how many hours would it take a human to find out?

And one more thing. Yeah, it’s freezing in London today ;)
